name: Orion
mythology: In Greek mythology, Orion was a great hunter placed among the stars, often depicted facing the charging bull Taurus, accompanied by his hunting dogs (Canis Major and Canis Minor).

notable_stars.name: Betelgeuse
notable_stars.description: A red supergiant marking Orion's shoulder, one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.

notable_stars.name: Rigel
notable_stars.description: A blue supergiant marking Orion's foot, one of the most luminous stars known.

notable_stars.name: Alnilam, Alnitak, Mintaka
notable_stars.description: The three bright stars forming Orion's Belt.

best_viewing.hemisphere: Both (best from Northern Hemisphere winter skies)
best_viewing.notes: Easiest to find via the three-star belt.

name: Ursa Major
mythology: One of the most recognizable star patterns, containing the asterism known as the Big Dipper (or Plough), used for millennia to find true north via the Pointer Stars.

notable_stars.name: Dubhe
notable_stars.description: One of the two 'Pointer Stars' used to locate Polaris.

notable_stars.name: Alkaid
notable_stars.description: Marks the end of the Dipper's handle.

notable_stars.name: Mizar & Alcor
notable_stars.description: A famous naked-eye double star in the handle.

best_viewing.notes: Circumpolar for most of North America and Europe.

name: Ursa Minor
mythology: Contains Polaris, the North Star, which sits nearly still in the sky as Earth rotates, making it a historic navigation aid.

notable_stars.name: Polaris
notable_stars.description: The North Star — nearly aligned with Earth's rotational axis.

notable_stars.name: Kochab
notable_stars.description: A bright orange giant in the bowl of the Little Dipper.

best_viewing.notes: Fainter than Ursa Major; follow the Pointer Stars to find Polaris.

name: Cassiopeia
mythology: Named for a vain queen in Greek mythology, recognizable by its distinctive W (or M) shape formed by five bright stars.

notable_stars.name: Schedar
notable_stars.description: An orange giant marking one point of the W.

notable_stars.name: Caph
notable_stars.description: A bright white giant at one end of the constellation.

best_viewing.notes: Circumpolar; sits opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris.

name: Scorpius
mythology: In Greek myth, the scorpion sent to kill Orion — the two constellations are never visible in the sky at the same time, forever chasing one another.

notable_stars.name: Antares
notable_stars.description: A red supergiant marking the scorpion's heart, one of the largest known stars.

notable_stars.name: Shaula
notable_stars.description: Marks the venomous stinger at the tail's tip.

best_viewing.hemisphere: Southern (visible low in southern sky from north)
best_viewing.notes: Look low on the southern horizon from northern latitudes.

name: Taurus
mythology: Represents a bull in Greek mythology; contains the Pleiades and Hyades star clusters, among the closest open clusters to Earth.

notable_stars.name: Aldebaran
notable_stars.description: An orange giant marking the bull's fiery red eye.

notable_stars.name: Pleiades (M45)
notable_stars.description: A famous open star cluster, sometimes called the Seven Sisters.

best_viewing.notes: Aldebaran and the V-shaped Hyades cluster form the bull's face.

name: Gemini
mythology: Represents the twin brothers Castor and Pollux from Greek mythology, marked by two bright stars of the same names at their heads.

notable_stars.name: Castor
notable_stars.description: A multiple-star system marking one twin's head.

notable_stars.name: Pollux
notable_stars.description: The brighter of the two twin stars, an orange giant with a known exoplanet.

best_viewing.notes: Found near Orion and Taurus in the winter sky.

name: Leo
mythology: Represents the Nemean Lion slain by Hercules in Greek mythology; its stars trace a distinctive backward-question-mark 'sickle' shape for the lion's head and mane.

notable_stars.name: Regulus
notable_stars.description: A blue-white star marking the lion's heart, one of the brightest stars in the night sky.

notable_stars.name: Denebola
notable_stars.description: Marks the tip of the lion's tail.

best_viewing.notes: Look for the backward question-mark 'Sickle' asterism.

name: Cygnus
mythology: Represents a swan in flight along the Milky Way, also known as the Northern Cross for the shape formed by its brightest stars.

notable_stars.name: Deneb
notable_stars.description: A blue-white supergiant marking the swan's tail, one of the most luminous stars known.

notable_stars.name: Albireo
notable_stars.description: A striking gold-and-blue double star marking the swan's head.

best_viewing.notes: Deneb forms one corner of the 'Summer Triangle' with Vega and Altair.

name: Lyra
mythology: Represents the lyre of Orpheus in Greek mythology, a small but distinctive constellation anchored by the brilliant star Vega.

notable_stars.name: Vega
notable_stars.description: One of the brightest stars in the night sky and a former (and future) pole star due to axial precession.

best_viewing.notes: Vega anchors the 'Summer Triangle' with Deneb and Altair.
